Reuters reported that Apple successfully defeated a proposed class-action lawsuit accusing the company of failing to prevent child sexual abuse material (CSAM) from being stored and shared via iCloud. Details as follows.

Apple is protected under Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act

According to Reuters, U.S. District Court Judge Noël Wise has dismissed a proposed class-action lawsuit filed in 2024, ruling that the case cannot be refiled. The lawsuit accused Apple of "failing to prevent the dissemination of child sexual abuse material through its iCloud data storage platform."

In the complaint, two abuse survivors identified under the pseudonyms Amy and Jessica alleged that images of their childhood abuse continue to circulate through iCloud, and that Apple deliberately refused to use available tools to detect and report known child sexual abuse material.

The lawsuit specifically highlighted Apple's decision to abandon NeuralHash — a system Apple announced in 2021, originally designed to match images uploaded to iCloud against databases of identified child abuse material.

Amy and Jessica sought to represent several thousand other survivors in the class action. Citing subsequent court filings, Reuters noted that the proposed class is estimated to involve 2,680 individuals, with "estimated damages potentially reaching $32.8 billion."

They argued that members of the proposed class were all affected by the same Apple policies and product decisions, and that consolidating their claims would reduce the burden and trauma of individual lawsuits. The complaint stated:

Returning to the court's dismissal ruling, Reuters noted that Judge Wise stated that "the lawsuit's attempt to hold Apple liable for failing to remove or block user-generated content falls within the scope of Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act." Section 230 is a federal law enacted in 1996.

In short, Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act generally shields online service providers from being held legally liable as publishers for content created by their users. The provision has long been at the centre of debate over how much responsibility tech companies should bear for content shared on their platforms.

Reuters noted that although the case has been ruled non-refilable, "lead counsel for the plaintiffs, James Marsh, said they are considering an appeal and evaluating other viable legal claims."
